concepts.definition: A network of lymphatic vessels, lymphoid tissues, and organs that returns interstitial fluid to blood, supports immune defense, and transports absorbed intestinal fats.
The fluid component of blood within blood vessels, containing water, dissolved ions, proteins, and other solutes.
Extracellular fluid occupying spaces between tissue cells before entering lymphatic vessels.
Interstitial fluid after it has entered a lymphatic vessel, generally containing fewer plasma proteins than blood plasma.
Maintenance of appropriate fluid distribution between blood, tissues, and lymphatic circulation.
Movement of fluid out of blood capillaries into tissues, influenced by fluid pressures and permeability.
The pressure exerted by fluid that helps drive filtration across capillary walls.
The osmotic influence of plasma proteins, especially albumin, that tends to retain or draw water into blood vessels.
Excess fluid accumulation in interstitial tissues, producing swelling.
Tissue swelling caused by impaired lymphatic drainage.
Monitoring tissues, lymph, and blood for pathogens or abnormal cells by immune cells.
Transport of many absorbed long-chain dietary fats from intestinal lacteals through lymphatics to venous blood.
Lipid-rich lymph originating in intestinal lacteals after absorption of a fatty meal.
Blood returning toward the heart through veins; the destination of lymphatic drainage.
Blind-ended, highly permeable small lymphatic vessel that takes in interstitial fluid and particulate material.
A tube that begins as a closed-end pocket rather than forming a continuous blood-like capillary loop.
Overlapping endothelial cell edges in initial lymphatics that open with favorable tissue pressure and resist outward leakage.
Connective-tissue attachment that helps keep a lymphatic capillary open as neighboring tissue swells.
Ability of initial lymphatics to admit fluid, large molecules, and some cells more readily than ordinary blood capillaries.
Downstream lymphatic conduit with valves and contractile walls that carries lymph toward trunks and ducts.
A one-way valve that limits reverse flow in collecting lymphatic vessels.
Segment of a collecting lymphatic vessel between consecutive valves that can contract to propel lymph.
Compression of lymphatic vessels during body movement that helps move lymph past one-way valves.
Breathing-related pressure differences in thorax and abdomen that assist lymph return.
Rhythmic contraction of lymphatic collecting-vessel smooth muscle that helps move fluid.
Specialized lymphatic capillary within an intestinal villus that takes up chylomicrons after dietary fat absorption.
Lipoprotein particle assembled in intestinal enterocytes to transport absorbed dietary triglycerides through lymph.
Tube carrying lymph toward larger lymphatic trunks and venous circulation, typically with directional valves.
Large collecting vessel that drains lymph from a defined body region into a lymphatic duct or major junction.
Lymphatic trunk draining much of the head and neck on its respective side.
Lymphatic trunk draining lymph from the ipsilateral upper limb.
Lymphatic trunk draining portions of the thorax, including thoracic viscera and associated structures.
Right or left large lymphatic trunk draining lower limb and pelvic/abdominal territories toward the cisterna chyli or thoracic duct.
Large lymphatic trunk carrying lymph, including absorbed intestinal lipids, from abdominal digestive organs toward the cisterna chyli/thoracic duct.
Short duct that typically drains the right upper quadrant: right head/neck, upper limb, and thorax.
Main lymphatic duct returning lymph from most of the body except the right upper quadrant.
Dilated lymphatic reservoir near the start of the thoracic duct, typically receiving lumbar and intestinal lymphatic trunks.
Junction of right internal jugular and right subclavian veins, a usual entry site for right upper-quadrant lymph.
Junction of left internal jugular and left subclavian veins, a usual termination of the thoracic duct.
Collection of lymph from the right side of head/neck, right upper limb, and right thorax, usually via the right lymphatic duct or separate trunks.
Both lower limbs, abdomen and pelvis, and the left upper quadrant of the body.
Encapsulated secondary lymphoid organ that filters lymph and brings antigens together with immune cells.
Outer connective-tissue covering of a lymph node.
Connective-tissue projection from the capsule into the node interior.
Indented region where efferent lymphatic vessels exit and blood vessels travel.
Vessel conveying lymph into a lymph node, usually through its convex surface.
Vessel carrying filtered lymph away from a node near its hilum.
Lymph-filled space immediately deep to the lymph node capsule; receives afferent lymph.
Superficial region that contains B-cell-rich lymphoid follicles.
Localized aggregate of lymphocytes, often enriched in B cells and potentially containing a germinal center.
Activated B-cell region in a secondary follicle where proliferation and affinity maturation occur.
Deep cortical area enriched in T lymphocytes and specialized venules.
Inner region containing medullary cords and sinuses.
Lymphocyte/plasma-cell-rich strand of tissue in a lymph node medulla.
Channel through the lymph node medulla that conveys lymph toward the efferent vessel.
Fluid route from the subcapsular sinus through cortical/trabecular and medullary sinuses to an efferent vessel.
Specialized blood vessel in lymphoid tissue allowing many circulating lymphocytes to enter a lymph node from blood.
Cell that carries and displays antigen-derived peptides to T cells, helping initiate adaptive immunity.
Formation of blood cells from hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, principally in red bone marrow.
Production and development of lymphocytes from hematopoietic precursor cells.
Primary lymphoid tissue that produces lymphocyte precursors and supports B-cell development.
Adaptive immune cell that can differentiate into antibody-producing plasma cells and memory B cells.
Adaptive immune cell that matures in the thymus and mediates cellular immune regulation or killing.
Innate lymphocyte that detects and kills certain infected, stressed, or transformed cells without a clonally rearranged antigen receptor.
Encapsulated primary lymphoid organ where developing T cells mature and undergo selection.
Immature developing T lymphocyte inside the thymus.
Outer part of a thymic lobule, densely populated with developing thymocytes.
Inner, paler part of a thymic lobule involved in selection and final maturation stages.
Specialized stromal cell organizing T-cell development and contributing to central tolerance.
Protective barrier prominent in the thymic cortex that limits exposure of immature thymocytes to circulating antigens.
Concentric whorl of thymic epithelial cells in the thymic medulla.
Thymic checkpoint retaining developing T cells able to recognize self-MHC sufficiently to function.
Thymic checkpoint that eliminates or redirects many developing T cells binding self-antigens too strongly.
Immune self-tolerance mechanisms established during lymphocyte development in primary lymphoid tissues.
Name for thymus-associated signaling peptides involved in T-cell development; does not establish a single universal B-cell differentiation hormone.
Age-associated shrinkage and replacement of much thymic lymphoid tissue by fatty/connective tissue.
Largest lymphoid organ; monitors blood, supports responses to blood-borne antigens, and removes aging or damaged red blood cells.
Connective-tissue covering surrounding the spleen.
Supportive connective-tissue band extending inward from the splenic capsule.
Visceral-surface indentation where the splenic artery and vein enter or leave.
Artery supplying the spleen with blood to be filtered and surveyed.
Vessel draining venous blood from the spleen toward the portal venous system.
Immune-cell-rich regions surrounding branches of splenic arteries, involved in recognition of blood-borne antigens.
Blood-rich splenic tissue that filters circulating blood and removes damaged erythrocytes.
Arterial branch associated with periarteriolar lymphoid tissue of the white pulp.
Splenic removal and phagocytic breakdown of aged or structurally abnormal erythrocytes.
Recovery of iron from dismantled erythrocyte hemoglobin for later reuse.
Smooth convex splenic surface conforming to the diaphragm.
Splenic surface bearing impressions related to nearby abdominal organs, including the stomach.
Surgical removal of the spleen, potentially increasing susceptibility to certain invasive infections.
Bacteria surrounded by polysaccharide capsules, against which splenic immune clearance is especially important.
Organized lymphocyte-rich structure with an anatomical capsule in the instructor's comparison, such as node, thymus, or spleen.
Lymphocyte-rich tissue that may lack a distinct enclosing organ capsule.
Site where immune lymphocytes are generated or mature, especially bone marrow and thymus.
Site where mature immune cells encounter antigens, including nodes and spleen.
Lymphoid tissue positioned at mucosal surfaces to monitor antigens arriving through the respiratory, gastrointestinal, or related tracts.
Intestinal mucosal immune tissue, including Peyer's patches and other gut lymphoid sites.
Lymphoid tissue associated with the bronchial mucosa.
Lymphoid tissue of nasal mucosal immune defense.
Organized lymphoid tissue in the pharyngeal region that samples incoming pathogens.
Paired tonsil along the lateral oropharynx, near the boundary between mouth and throat.
Tonsillar lymphoid tissue on the roof/posterior wall of the nasopharynx, often called the adenoid.
Lymphoid tissue near the posterior base of the tongue.
Ring of tonsillar lymphoid tissue surrounding entry to the pharynx.
Aggregated lymphoid follicles, especially in the ileum, supporting intestinal immune surveillance.
Cecal appendage containing substantial lymphoid tissue and capable of inflammation called appendicitis.
Specialized intestinal epithelial cell that transports luminal antigen toward underlying mucosal immune tissue.
Rapid defense using inherited recognition pathways; traditionally taught as nonspecific immunity.
Skin, intact mucosa, and protective secretions limiting pathogen entry.
Engulfment and intracellular digestion of particles, pathogens, or cellular debris.
Rapidly recruited granulocyte that phagocytoses microbes during acute inflammation.
Blood-circulating leukocyte that can differentiate into macrophages or related tissue cells.
Tissue phagocyte involved in debris clearance, inflammatory signaling, and some antigen presentation.
Immune sentinel specialized in antigen capture and presentation to T lymphocytes.
Elimination of certain abnormal cells by NK-cell granule release and other killing pathways.
NK-cell detection of reduced or altered self-MHC class I signals in some abnormal cells.
Cytotoxic-granule protein that helps granzymes reach a target cell to initiate death.
Cytotoxic serine protease released by NK and CD8 T cells that can promote target-cell apoptosis.
Controlled programmed cell death that can remove damaged, infected, or dangerous cells.
Innate and adaptive monitoring of tissues and fluids for abnormal or foreign material.
Pathogen or tumor strategy that limits immune recognition or killing.
Protective response mediated by immune cells, especially T-cell-dependent functions, rather than secreted antibodies alone.
Coordinated tissue response to injury or infection involving changes in blood flow, permeability, and immune-cell recruitment.
Redness, a classic cardinal sign of inflammation primarily associated with increased local blood flow.
Heat, a classic cardinal sign of inflammation associated with increased local blood flow.
Swelling, a classic sign of inflammation associated with increased vascular permeability and fluid movement into tissue.
Pain, a classic cardinal sign of inflammation due to inflammatory mediators and tissue pressure/injury.
Loss of function, sometimes counted as a fifth clinical sign of inflammation beyond the instructor's four.
Widening of blood vessels, increasing local blood flow.
Ease with which blood vessel walls permit fluid and certain molecules to move into tissues.
Tissue-resident immune cell that can release histamine and other mediators during inflammation and allergy.
Inflammatory mediator that can promote local vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.
Directed immune-cell movement along a chemical gradient toward a signal source.
Passage of leukocytes across a blood-vessel wall into tissue.
Regulated rise in the body's temperature set point, commonly as part of systemic response to infection/inflammation.
Substance or signaling mediator that promotes fever through effects on thermoregulation.
Brain region participating in thermoregulatory control, including fever responses.
Inflammatory lipid mediator important in raising the hypothalamic temperature set point during fever.
Secreted signaling protein that coordinates immune-cell activity and inflammatory responses.
Cytokine family, including antiviral type I interferons, that induces defense programs in nearby cells.
Antiviral cytokines such as IFN-alpha and IFN-beta that stimulate expression of antiviral proteins.
Cascade of plasma proteins that can tag pathogens, recruit inflammation, and assemble a membrane attack complex.
Complement activation route often triggered by antibodies bound to their targets.
Complement route triggered by recognition of microbial carbohydrate patterns.
Complement amplification/activation pathway on appropriate microbial surfaces.
Complement fragment that helps coat pathogens for phagocytosis, a form of opsonization.
Complement-derived inflammatory mediator produced during cascade activation.
Potent complement inflammatory and chemotactic mediator.
Complement protein assembly that can form pores in susceptible target membranes.
Coating a target with molecules such as IgG or C3b to promote phagocytic recognition and uptake.
Blocking a pathogen's or toxin's harmful interaction with host cells, often by antibody binding.
Clumping of particles or cells after antibodies crosslink their surface antigens.
Formation of insoluble aggregates when antibodies crosslink soluble antigens.
Molecular structure recognized by an immune receptor or processed for display as peptide by MHC molecules.
Cell displaying antigen-derived peptides bound to MHC molecules for recognition by T cells.
Cell-surface proteins that present peptides for T-cell recognition.
Peptide-presenting molecule expressed by nearly all nucleated cells and recognized by CD8 T cells.
Peptide-presenting molecule normally concentrated on professional antigen-presenting cells and recognized by CD4 T cells.
T lymphocyte often specializing in cytotoxic killing after recognizing peptides presented on MHC I.
T lymphocyte recognizing peptide–MHC II and coordinating immune responses through signaling and cell contact.
Antigen-specific receptor that recognizes particular peptide–MHC complexes.
Additional activating signal often required along with T-cell antigen recognition to initiate a full naive T-cell response.
Proliferation of an activated antigen-specific lymphocyte population.
Target-cell destruction through mechanisms such as perforin/granzyme release or death-receptor signaling.
T-cell population that suppresses inappropriate immune activation and supports tolerance.
Persistence of antigen-experienced T lymphocytes capable of responding more rapidly after reexposure.
Combination of a processed peptide antigen with an MHC molecule on a cell surface.
Display of processed antigenic fragments by MHC molecules for T-cell recognition.
Membrane immunoglobulin recognizing an antigen in native form on a B lymphocyte.
Differentiated B-cell descendant specialized for secreting large quantities of antibody.
Antigen-experienced B lymphocyte able to respond during later exposure.
Adaptive immunity mediated mainly by antibodies circulating in body fluids.
Immunoglobulin secreted by plasma cells that binds specific antigenic determinants.
Specific antigenic site recognized by an antibody or immune receptor; for antibodies often a surface molecular feature.
Immunoglobulin region providing much of an antibody's antigen-binding specificity.
Immunoglobulin region helping determine antibody isotype and effector interactions.
One of two larger identical polypeptide chains in a typical antibody molecule.
One of two smaller identical polypeptide chains in a typical antibody molecule.
Antigen-recognition region at each arm of a typical Y-shaped antibody.
Constant region of an antibody that interacts with immune receptors or complement components.
Major serum antibody class that supports neutralization, opsonization, and several other protective functions.
Antibody class typically secreted early during a primary response; secreted IgM often forms pentamers.
Antibody class prominent in mucosal secretions such as saliva, tears, and intestinal mucus.
Antibody class central to immediate allergic responses and some defenses against parasites.
Immunoglobulin class found primarily as an antigen receptor on many naive mature B cells.
B-cell DNA rearrangement allowing a change in antibody constant region/isotype while retaining antigen specificity.
Selection of B-cell variants producing antibodies with progressively stronger antigen binding.
Antigen-specific immune responses mediated mainly by B and T cells, capable of memory.
Ability of adaptive immune receptors to distinguish particular antigenic structures.
Capacity to recognize a very large range of distinct antigens through diverse lymphocyte receptors.
Mechanisms preventing harmful immune attack on self or innocuous targets.
Persistent lymphocytes and/or antibody-producing cells that support improved responses after prior exposure.
Protection generated by an individual's own antigen-specific immune response.
Protection provided by transferred antibodies without the recipient initially generating that response.
Adaptive protection developed following infection/exposure rather than deliberate immunization.
Adaptive protection induced by vaccination.
Transfer of protective antibodies from mother to child through placenta or breast milk.
Protection supplied by administration of preformed antibodies or immunoglobulins.
Initial adaptive response to an antigen, typically with a lag before substantial antibody production.
Memory-influenced response to previously encountered antigen, generally faster and often stronger.
Measure of antibody amount or activity in a specimen, often assessed through serial dilutions.
Deliberate exposure to antigen or an antigen-producing platform to elicit protective adaptive immunity.
Disease driven by immune responses that inappropriately damage the body's own tissues.
Human immunodeficiency virus, which targets CD4 T cells and can cause progressive immunodeficiency without effective treatment.
Advanced clinical syndrome caused by HIV-associated immune impairment, diagnosed using defined clinical/immunologic criteria.
Inflammation of the vermiform appendix that may progress to perforation and peritonitis.
